newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court rules for GM Hughes unit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court rules for GM Hughes unit.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled Monday for a unit of General Motors Corp.'s Hughes Electronics, dismissing a whistleblower lawsuit against the defence contractor on technical grounds.

The case stemmed from a 1989 suit by William Schumer, a former Hughes Aircraft Co. manager, alleging the firm in 1982-84 mischarged costs from a fixed-price contract for F-15 aircraft to the cost-reimbursement contract for B-2 aircraft.
He sought $150 million in damages. The Justice Department declined to join the civil lawsuit.

A federal judge in California dismissed the lawsuit. But a U.S. Court of Appeals reinstated the parts of the suit alleging that Hughes failed to properly disclose the terms of its agreements and did not comply with the disclosure requirements under cost accounting standards.
In a unanimous Supreme Court ruling, Justice Clarence Thomas said 1986 changes in the law do not apply retroactively to alleged false claims that took place before then.
"We hold that the 1986 amendment does not apply to this action and therefore that this action should have been dismissed, as required by the 1982 version of the act," he wrote in the 12-page ruling.

Prior to 1986, such suits were barred if the information on which they were based already was in the government's possession. Hughes Aircraft contended the suit was based on the public disclosure of allegations in an administrative audit.
Supporting the company's appeal were the U.S. Chamber of Commerce business group and trade associations representing aircraft manufactuers, shipbuilders and the electronics industry.
The Justice Department supported the law as constitutional and urged the high court to reject the company's appeal.
